result: A MOR knockout rat model was generated and validated. The knockout animals showed no opioid-induced currents or hyperpolarization in LC neurons, while other G protein-coupled receptors (alpha-2-adrenoceptors, orphanin FQ, M3-muscarine receptors) functioned normally.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 describe the generation and genotyping validation of the knockout model. Claims C13-C14 provide functional validation showing selective loss of MOR signaling while preserving other GPCR responses. The data demonstrate successful and specific knockout of MOR.

result: Virally expressed exWT and TPD receptors in MOR knockout rats showed normal acute activation kinetics comparable to endogenous receptors. Multiple measures of activation (rise time, time to peak, deactivation kinetics) were statistically indistinguishable between exWT, TPD, and wild-type receptors, and chronic morphine treatment did not alter activation kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C15-C17, C19-C20 provide quantitative electrophysiology data with appropriate statistical tests (unpaired t-tests, ANOVA) showing no significant differences in activation parameters between receptor types. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-17 per group). Claims C55-C56 confirm activation kinetics are unchanged by morphine treatment. The conclusion (C21, C65) that TPD mutations do not affect acute G protein signaling is well-supported.

result: TPD receptors showed markedly reduced acute desensitization compared to exWT receptors. During ME application, exWT receptors desensitized to 54-75% of peak while TPD receptors maintained 80-94% of peak response. Recovery from desensitization was also dramatically impaired in exWT (23-30% recovery) but largely preserved in TPD receptors (76-81% recovery).
evaluation: Claims C22-C29 provide comprehensive quantitative data from both intracellular and whole-cell recordings with appropriate statistical comparisons (unpaired t-tests, one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.0001-0.0004). Sample sizes are adequate (n=5-13). Two independent recording methods and two measures of desensitization converge on the same conclusion (C30). The data strongly support reduced desensitization in TPD receptors.

result: PKC-mediated heterologous desensitization induced by muscarine was not blocked by C-terminal phosphorylation site mutations. Muscarine similarly reduced MOR responses in both exWT and TPD receptors, indicating PKC acts through a mechanism independent of C-terminal phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36 provide quantitative data showing muscarine reduces responses similarly in exWT and TPD receptors. Claim C35 shows muscarine more than doubles the small desensitization seen in TPD (p=0.0009). The conclusion (C37, C76-C77) that PKC acts independently of C-terminal phosphorylation is logically supported by the observation that TPD receptors remain sensitive to muscarine despite lacking C-terminal phosphorylation sites.

result: ME-induced internalization was completely disrupted in TPD receptors. ExWT receptors showed 38±3% internalization while TPD receptors showed only 10±5% internalization (p=0.0004), measured using fluorescently-tagged anti-GFP nanobodies to label surface receptors.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 provide quantitative imaging data with statistical comparison (unpaired t-test, p=0.0004) and adequate sample sizes (n=6-7). Claim C103 describes the validated method for selective labeling of surface receptors. The conclusion (C40) that internalization is completely disrupted is strongly supported, though 'completely' may be slightly overstated given 10% residual signal.

result: Following chronic morphine treatment (80 mg/kg/day for 6-7 days), exWT receptors internalized (49±6%) while TPD receptors showed no internalization (0%, p=0.002). The inability of TPD receptors to internalize was maintained after chronic morphine exposure.
evaluation: Claims C42-C43 provide quantitative imaging data with statistical comparison and adequate sample sizes (n=4 per group). Claim C102 describes the chronic morphine treatment protocol. The data demonstrate that TPD receptors remain resistant to internalization even after chronic morphine treatment, supporting the conclusion in C44.

result: ExWT receptors developed cellular tolerance following chronic morphine treatment, evidenced by increased acute desensitization (59% vs 41% remaining current, p=0.001) and impaired recovery from desensitization (35% vs 13% recovery at 5 min, p=0.01). The recovery time course was significantly delayed (p=0.0001, two-way ANOVA).
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 provide quantitative data with appropriate statistical tests (unpaired t-tests, two-way ANOVA) comparing untreated and morphine-treated animals. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-8). The data demonstrate two independent measures of tolerance in exWT receptors, supporting the conclusion in C51 and C104.

result: TPD receptors did not develop cellular tolerance following chronic morphine treatment. All measures of opioid action (desensitization during ME application, recovery from desensitization, response to repeated photolysis) were unchanged between untreated and morphine-treated animals expressing TPD receptors.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 show no statistical differences in desensitization or recovery measures (p=0.34, two-way ANOVA). Claims C57-C62 provide additional evidence from photolysis experiments showing exWT but not TPD receptors exhibit desensitization after prolonged agonist exposure. Sample sizes are adequate (n=9-13). The convergence of multiple independent measures strongly supports the conclusion that TPD receptors do not develop tolerance.

result: C-terminal phosphorylation is necessary for acute desensitization, receptor trafficking, and cellular tolerance to morphine. Elimination of all C-terminal phosphorylation sites rendered MORs resistant to these adaptive processes while preserving acute G protein signaling.
evaluation: This overarching conclusion integrates the major findings from desensitization (C22-C30), internalization (C38-C44), and tolerance (C46-C62) experiments. The data consistently show that TPD receptors lack these adaptive responses while maintaining normal acute function. The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

result: Tolerance development in locus coeruleus is cell autonomous, as demonstrated by localized viral expression of receptors specifically in LC neurons showing tolerance without requiring receptor activation in other CNS areas.
evaluation: The experimental design using localized viral injection (C100-C101) combined with the observation of tolerance in exWT-expressing neurons (C47-C51) supports this conclusion. However, the claim would be strengthened by explicit controls or discussion of potential circuit-level effects.

result: MOR desensitization and internalization are mechanistically distinct processes that can be dissociated by the degree of C-terminal phosphorylation. Mutations in STANT reduce internalization without eliminating desensitization, while mutation of both TSST and STANT (or all phosphosites) is required to substantially reduce desensitization.
evaluation: Claims C2-C6 establish the background on phosphorylation sites from prior literature. Claims C69-C75 synthesize evidence from multiple cited studies (Lau et al., 2011; Birdsong et al., 2015; Arttamangkul et al., 2006; Yousuf et al., 2015) showing dissociation between desensitization and internalization. The current study's findings with TPD receptors (showing both processes eliminated) are consistent with this framework.

result: PKC-mediated facilitation of MOR desensitization may result from phosphorylation of intracellular loops rather than the C-terminus, or from phosphorylation of other signaling proteins. Evidence from different systems (HEK293 cells vs. LC neurons) shows inconsistent effects of muscarinic activation on MOR trafficking.
evaluation: Claims C78-C79 present alternative interpretations supported by citations, but these remain speculative. Claims C80-C81 note conflicting findings between cell culture and native tissue systems. The current study's data (C34-C37) support PKC acting independently of C-terminal phosphorylation, but the specific mechanism remains unclear.

result: TPD receptors function almost exclusively through G protein-dependent processes, lacking arrestin recruitment and internalization. Mutations eliminating C-terminal phosphorylation sites prevent arrestin association while preserving G protein signaling (adenylyl cyclase inhibition, GIRK activation).
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 synthesize evidence from prior studies (Lau et al., 2011; Just et al., 2013) and the current work showing TPD receptors lack internalization but maintain G protein signaling. The characterization as 'G protein biased' (C87) is a reasonable interpretation, though this is an inference rather than direct measurement of arrestin recruitment in the current study.

result: The lack of tolerance in TPD receptors may result from either the block of desensitization alone or the elimination of arrestin-mediated internalization. Longer morphine treatment might reveal slower tolerance development or compensatory homeostatic mechanisms. Evidence from arrestin3-null mice suggests internalization/recycling dynamics contribute to tolerance.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 present alternative interpretations of the tolerance data. Claims C89-C90 and C97 acknowledge limitations and speculate about potential outcomes with longer treatment. Claims C92-C93 cite supporting evidence from arrestin3-null mice. While the data clearly show TPD receptors lack tolerance at 6-7 days, the mechanistic interpretation and predictions about longer treatment remain speculative.

result: The study characterized acute activation, desensitization, endocytosis, and tolerance in LC neurons from MOR knockout rats expressing exWT and TPD receptors. ExWT receptors behaved similarly to endogenous receptors in wild-type animals.
evaluation: Claim C63 accurately summarizes the study scope. Claim C64 is supported by the activation kinetics data (C15-C21) and desensitization data (C22-C25) showing exWT receptors recapitulate wild-type behavior. This validates the experimental system.
